mainTopic: A pit covered for oxen but not camels: are camels that come occasionally negligence, and does negligence about camels carry over (מגו) to a cover that rotted?
overview: The גמרא asks what happens when a pit is covered well enough for oxen but not for camels. First it asks about camels that come only occasionally, weaken the cover, and then an ox falls in. It tries to answer from both clauses of the משנה, "covered properly, exempt" and "did not cover properly, liable." Both proofs are pushed off. The first clause may be about a cover that rotted from inside. The second clause may be about common camels, written only to match the first clause. A second version (איכא דאמרי) says the occasional-camels case is simply negligence. In that version the real question is מגו: if the owner was careless about common camels but the cover actually rotted, is he liable? Proofs from both clauses of the משנה are again pushed off. Finally a ברייתא about a deaf ox versus a sharp ox walking by day proves that we do not say מגו. The amud closes with רב explaining the משנה's words "forward" and "backward."

steps.title: Proof from the first clause: the owner is exempt
steps.stepSummary: The first clause of the משנה says a pit covered properly makes the owner פטור. The גמרא reads it as a cover fit for oxen but not camels, in a place where camels come occasionally. That would prove the owner is an אנוס.
steps.simpleTranslation: The case must be a cover fit for oxen but not for camels. If camels are common there, why would he be exempt? He was careless! If camels are never there, it's obvious he's exempt. So it must be a place where camels come once in a while. Camels came and weakened the cover, then oxen fell in, and the משנה says he is exempt. So since the camels aren't there now, he counts as not at fault.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a proof from the משנה's first line, "covered properly … exempt." It argues this line must be about our exact question, and the answer is "exempt."
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא rules out two readings. If camels are common, he is clearly a פושע, so he couldn't be exempt. If camels never come, the ruling would be too obvious to teach. The only case left is the "in-between" one, camels coming occasionally. Since the משנה says פטור there, the owner counts as an אנוס.

keyTerms.meaning: Negligent: someone who was careless and is therefore responsible.
Someone who could not have prevented what happened, so he is not at fault.
It is obvious, so why would it need to be taught?
Rather, is it not…? This introduces the only reading that is left.

steps.confusionAlert: This step begins in the middle of a sentence. The words before it (on the previous lines) were: "Rather, is it not a case where he covered it properly for oxen…"

phrases.english: but not appropriately for camels?
And if it is where camels are commonly found,
why is he exempt? He is negligent!
And if camels are not commonly found there –
it is obvious; he is a victim of circumstance!
Rather, is it not where camels come occasionally,
and camels came and weakened it,
and then oxen came and fell into it –
and it teaches that he is exempt?
Apparently, since now the camels are not there –
he is a victim of circumstance!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the first proof attempt, which began just before this section, for the question about camels.
steps.raayaObject: The open question: a cover fit for oxen but not camels, weakened by camels that come occasionally, and then an ox falls in.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה's first clause: "כסהו כראוי … פטור".

steps.title: Rejected: the cover rotted from inside
steps.stepSummary: The proof is pushed off. The משנה's "covered properly" means properly even for camels. The ox fell because the cover rotted from inside, as רבי יצחק בר בר חנה explains.
steps.simpleTranslation: They answered: No. Really it means a cover good enough for oxen and good enough for camels. And as for your question, "So how did the ox fall in?": רבי יצחק בר בר חנה says it was a case where the cover rotted from the inside.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof from step 1. It shows another way to read the משנה's case that has nothing to do with camels.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof depended on the claim that a cover good even for camels could never let an ox fall through. רבי יצחק בר בר חנה gives a way it could happen: the cover rotted from inside, which nobody could see. So the first clause is about a true אנוס case and teaches nothing about our question.

keyTerms.meaning: Really / actually. This goes back to the simple reading.

phrases.english: They said: No,
actually it was covered properly for oxen and properly for camels;
and as for what was difficult for you – how did they fall?

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יִצְחָק בַּר בַּר חָנָה:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yitzchak bar bar Chana said:
where it rotted from the inside.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרִי: לָא, לְעוֹלָם כָּרָאוּי לִשְׁווֹרִים וְכָרָאוּי לִגְמַלִּים
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole proof from the first clause.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: It assumed an ox could only fall through a cover that was weak for camels. A cover can also rot from inside, which nobody could foresee.

steps.title: A new proof from the second clause: setting up the case
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tries the משנה's second clause: "did not cover properly … liable." It rules out the case of a cover too weak for oxen too, since that would be obvious. Then it starts narrowing down the cover fit for oxen but not camels.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: If he did not cover it properly, and an ox or donkey fell in and died, he is liable. What's the case? If the cover wasn't good enough for oxen or for camels, that's obvious. Do we need to be told he's liable? So isn't it a cover good for oxen but not for camels? Now, what's the case? If camels are common there, he is careless. If camels are never there, he is not at fault.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a second proof attempt, now from the משנה's second clause. This step is setting up the case. The actual proof comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Just as before, the גמרא says the simple case (a cover too weak even for oxen) is too obvious to teach. So the clause must be about a cover fit for oxen but not camels. Then it rules out both extremes. If camels are common, liability is obvious. If camels never come, he would be an אנוס and could not be liable.

keyTerms.meaning: What are the circumstances? What exactly is the case?
If you say… This offers a reading that will then be rejected.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
If he did not cover it properly,

phrases.aramaic: וְנָפַל לְתוֹכוֹ שׁוֹר אוֹ חֲמוֹר, וָמֵת – חַיָּיב.
phrases.english: and an ox or a donkey fell into it and died – he is liable.
What are the circumstances?
If we say it was not covered properly for oxen
and not properly for camels,
it is obvious – does it need to be said that he is liable?!
Rather, is it not covered properly for oxen
but not properly for camels?
What are the circumstances?
If camels are commonly found – he is negligent!
phrases.notes: So it would be too obvious to need teaching.

phrases.aramaic: וְאִי דְּלָא שְׁכִיחִי גְּמַלִּים – אָנוּס הוּא!
phrases.english: And if camels are not commonly found – he is a victim of circumstance!
phrases.notes: So how could the משנה call him liable?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the first proof was rejected, a new proof attempt opens from the משנה's next clause.
steps.raayaObject: The same question about camels that come occasionally.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה's second clause: "לא כסהו כראוי … חייב".

steps.title: Proof: occasional camels make him negligent
steps.stepSummary: The only case left is a place where camels come occasionally. Since the משנה says חייב, the owner is a פושע, because he should have expected the camels.
steps.simpleTranslation: So isn't it a place where camels come once in a while? Camels came and weakened the cover, then oxen came and fell in, and the משנה says he is liable. So since camels do come sometimes, he is careless. He should have thought about them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the second proof. It says the second clause is about our exact case, and the ruling is "liable."
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא repeats the same picture as step 1 word for word, but now the משנה's ruling is חייב, not פטור. Its reason is that if camels come even sometimes, the owner should have planned for them. That makes him a פושע. This is the opposite of what step 1 tried to prove.

keyTerms.meaning: Apparently. This draws the conclusion of a proof.
To bring to mind; to think ahead about something.

steps.whatToRemember: Read this way, the second clause of the משנה would show that a pit owner is a פושע if camels come even occasionally. The next step pushes this proof off.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the opposite of the proof in step 1. Step 5 pushes this proof off too, so the משנה ends up proving nothing about camels that come occasionally.

phrases.english: Rather, is it not where camels come occasionally,
and camels came and weakened it,
and then oxen came and fell into it –
and it teaches that he is liable?

phrases.aramaic: אַלְמָא כֵּיוָן דְּאָתַיִין לִפְרָקִים – פּוֹשֵׁעַ הוּא,
phrases.english: Apparently, since they come occasionally – he is negligent,
since he should have kept it in mind!

steps.triggerLanguage: אַלְמָא כֵּיוָן דְּאָתַיִין לִפְרָקִים – פּוֹשֵׁעַ הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the proof set up in step 3. It uses the same wording as step 1 but reaches the opposite result.
steps.raayaObject: Whether a pit owner is responsible when camels that come occasionally weaken the cover and then an ox falls in.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה's second clause ("לא כסהו כראוי … חייב"), read as the case of camels that come occasionally.

steps.title: The second clause is really about common camels, worded to match the first clause
steps.stepSummary: The proof from 'did not cover properly … liable' is pushed off. The משנה is talking about a place where camels are common. That ruling is obvious, but the תנא wrote it only to match the wording of the first clause.
steps.simpleTranslation: Really, the case is a cover fit for oxen but not camels, in a place where camels are common. You asked why the משנה would teach something so obvious, since he is clearly a פושע. The answer: since the תנא wrote 'covered it properly' in the first clause, he also wrote 'did not cover it properly' in the second clause.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof from Step 4. It says the משנה's חייב case is where camels are common, not where they only come occasionally.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 3 had ruled out obvious cases, because a משנה should not teach something obvious. Now the גמרא answers that an obvious clause can appear just to balance the wording of the clause before it. So the occasional-camels case is not proven from the משנה either way.

keyTerms.meaning: Really / actually: introduces the true reading of the case
Since he wrote the first clause: the second clause is there to match the wording
The latter clause of a משנה

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the גמרא now holds that the משנה teaches something new here. It admits the clause is obvious and explains it is there only to match the first clause.

phrases.english: Really, it was appropriate for oxen
and not appropriate for camels,
and camels are commonly found there;
and as for what bothered you, that he is clearly negligent (so why teach it)!
phrases.notes: This goes back to Step 3, where the גמרא turned down a reading of the משנה because the ruling would be too obvious.

phrases.english: since he wrote the first clause, "he covered it properly,"
he wrote the latter clause too, "he did not cover it properly."

steps.triggerLanguage: לְעוֹלָם כָּרָאוּי לִשְׁווֹרִים וְלֹא כָּרָאוּי לִגְמַלִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof made in Step 4.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof from the סיפא that the occasional-camels case makes him a פושע.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed the obvious common-camels case could not be meant. But an obvious clause can be written just to match the first clause.

steps.title: Second version: the occasional-camels case was never in doubt
steps.stepSummary: An איכא דאמרי version says the owner is clearly a פושע when camels come occasionally, because he should have expected them. So that was never the question.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say: we certainly never asked about this case either. Since camels come there occasionally, he is a פושע, because he should have thought about it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a different version of the whole discussion. It says the occasional-camels case is simple: the owner is a פושע. This sets up the real question in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first version, the occasional-camels case was the open question. This version takes that case off the table, because expecting occasional visitors is the owner's job. So the question must be about something else.

keyTerms.meaning: To bring to mind, to expect

phrases.english: There are those who say:

phrases.aramaic: הָא נָמֵי וַדַּאי לָא אִיבַּעְיָא לַן;
phrases.english: this too we certainly did not ask about;
phrases.notes: "This too" means the case where camels come only occasionally.

phrases.english: since they come occasionally, he is negligent,
because he should have kept it in mind;

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא דְאָמְרִי: הָא נָמֵי וַדַּאי לָא אִיבַּעְיָא לַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a second version of the sugya instead of the proof-and-rejection cycle.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If camels come occasionally, a cover that cannot hold camels makes the owner a פושע.

steps.title: The real question: weak against common camels, but it rotted instead
steps.stepSummary: The cover could not hold camels, and camels are common there, so he is a פושע about camels. But the pit actually opened because the cover rotted from inside. Do we say מגו and make him liable for the rotting too?
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what we really asked: he covered it with a cover that can hold oxen but not camels, and camels are common there. The cover rotted from inside. What is the law? Do we say that since he is a פושע about camels, he is also a פושע about the rotting? Or perhaps we do not say מגו?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא states the real question in this second version. It asks whether negligence about one danger, the camels, makes the owner liable when the damage came from a different cause, the rotting.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Rotting from inside, on its own, is an אונס (Step 2). Here the owner was negligent, but the camels did not cause the accident. The question is whether his negligence carries over, through מגו, to the rotting that actually happened.

keyTerms.meaning: It rotted (became wormy) from the inside
Since: one status carries over to another situation

steps.whyThisMatters: This raises a basic question in נזיקין: if someone was negligent, is he responsible for damage that came about through an אונס that has nothing to do with his negligence?

phrases.aramaic: כִּי אִיבְּעִי לַן – הָכִי הוּא דְּאִיבַּעְיָא לַן:
phrases.english: when we asked, this is what we asked:

phrases.aramaic: כִּסָּהוּ כִּסּוּי שֶׁיָּכוֹל לַעֲמוֹד בִּפְנֵי שְׁווֹרִים
phrases.english: he covered it with a cover able to hold up against oxen
but unable to hold up against camels,
and camels are commonly found there;
and it rotted from inside: what is the law?

phrases.aramaic: מִי אָמְרִינַן: מִגּוֹ דְּהָוֵי פּוֹשֵׁעַ אֵצֶל גְּמַלִּים,
phrases.english: Do we say: since he is negligent regarding camels,
he is negligent also regarding the rotting;
or perhaps we do not say "since"?

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי אִיבְּעִי לַן – הָכִי הוּא דְּאִיבַּעְיָא לַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Having set aside the occasional-camels case in Step 6, the גמרא now states the real question.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether being a פושע about common camels makes the owner liable when the cover failed by rotting, which is an אונס.

steps.title: A proof begins from the משנה and רבי יצחק בר בר חנה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings the משנה: covered properly, an animal fell in and died, he is פטור. רבי יצחק בר בר חנה explained that the cover rotted from inside.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: if he covered it properly, and an ox or donkey fell in and died, he is פטור. And רבי יצחק בר בר חנה said about this: it is where the cover rotted from inside.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a proof for the question in Step 7. It quotes the משנה together with רבי יצחק בר בר חנה's explanation that the cover rotted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This text speaks about a cover that rotted from inside, which is exactly the situation in the question. The גמרא will now ask what kind of cover 'properly' means, to see whether it includes a cover too weak for camels.

keyTerms.meaning: And it was said about it: a later teacher's comment on a text

phrases.english: Come and hear:
if he covered it properly,

phrases.aramaic: וְנָפַל לְתוֹכוֹ שׁוֹר אוֹ חֲמוֹר, וָמֵת – פָּטוּר.
phrases.english: and an ox or a donkey fell into it and died, he is exempt.
And it was said about it,

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יִצְחָק בַּר בַּר חָנָה: שֶׁהִתְלִיעַ מִתּוֹכוֹ.
phrases.english: Rabbi Yitzchak bar bar Chana said: where it rotted from inside.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to answer the question from Step 7.
steps.raayaObject: Whether a מגו of פשיעה applies to rotting.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה 'כסהו כראוי … פטור' as explained by רבי יצחק בר בר חנה.

steps.title: Ruling out a cover fit even for camels
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what case the משנה means. A cover fit even for camels that rotted cannot be meant, because then he is obviously פטור. He could have done nothing more.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If you say it was proper for oxen and proper for camels, and it rotted from inside, it is obvious that he is פטור. What should he have done?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins narrowing down which cover the משנה means. It rules out a cover strong enough even for camels, because that ruling would be obvious.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the cover was fully proper and then rotted, the owner did nothing wrong, so there is nothing new to teach. This pushes toward reading the משנה as a cover too weak for camels, which would answer the question. The גמרא has not finished the proof yet.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? How does it look?
If you say: introduces a possible reading that will be tested
What should he have done? He is not at fault

phrases.english: What is the case?
If you say it was proper for oxen and proper for camels,
and it rotted from inside,
it is obvious that he is exempt;
what should he have done?

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵיכִי דָמֵי? אִילֵּימָא כָּרָאוּי לִשְׁווֹרִים וְכָרָאוּי לִגְמַלִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the proof by defining the case, ruling out the first option.
steps.raayaObject: That the משנה must be talking about a cover too weak for camels.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The rule that a משנה does not teach something obvious, so a cover fit even for camels is ruled out.

steps.title: The exempt case must be a cover too weak for camels that rotted, so no מגו
steps.stepSummary: Since the 'covered properly' case cannot mean a cover strong enough even for camels, it must mean a cover fit for oxen but not camels, where camels are common, and the cover rotted. The משנה says פטור, so we do not say מגו.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it must mean the cover was strong enough for oxen but not for camels, camels are common there, and it rotted from inside. And the משנה says he is exempt. So we see that we do not say: since he is negligent about camels, he is negligent about rotting too.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the proof it started in step 9. It decides which case the משנה must mean and draws the conclusion: no מגו.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 9 ruled out a cover fit even for camels, because then the exemption is obvious. So the case must be a cover that was too weak for camels in a place where camels are common. The משנה still says פטור when an ox fell in because the cover rotted, so his negligence about camels does not spill over to the rotting.

keyTerms.meaning: It rotted from the inside (literally, became wormy)

phrases.english: Rather, is it not a case where it was fit for oxen
but not fit for camels,
and camels are common there,
and it rotted from inside,
and the משנה teaches that he is exempt?
Apparently we do not say
that since he is negligent regarding camels
he is negligent regarding the rotting!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא לָאו כָּרָאוּי לִשְׁווֹרִים וְלֹא כָּרָאוּי לִגְמַלִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the proof begun in step 9 by picking the only remaining case.
steps.raayaObject: That we do not say מגו: negligence about camels does not make him liable for rotting.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה's clause 'covered properly … פטור', as explained by רבי יצחק בר בר חנה (it rotted from inside).

steps.title: The exempt case really is a cover fit for camels, and the new point is that he need not knock on it
steps.stepSummary: The proof is rejected. The משנה means a cover fit even for camels that rotted. It is not obvious, because you might have thought he had to knock on the cover to check it.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Really the cover was fit for camels and fit for oxen, and it rotted from inside. And as for what bothered you, that once it rotted there was nothing more he could have done: you might have said he should have gone and knocked on it to check. So the משנה teaches us that he did not have to.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes off the proof by going back to the case it rejected in step 9. It answers the 'that's obvious' problem by showing what the משנה is really teaching.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 9 said a cover fit for camels that rotted gives an obvious פטור. Now the גמרא says it is not obvious: maybe he had to tap the cover to check that it was not hollow. The משנה teaches that he did not, so the clause says nothing about מגו.

keyTerms.meaning: Really, actually (going back to an earlier option)
It teaches us (that this is not so)

phrases.english: No; really it was fit for camels
and fit for oxen,
and it rotted from inside.
And as for what was difficult for you:
phrases.notes: This points back to step 9's question, 'what more could he have done?'

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הִתְלִיעַ מַאי הֲוָה לֵיהּ לְמֶעְבַּד?
phrases.english: when it rotted, what should he have done?
You might have said
that he should have gone and knocked on it;
so it teaches us that he did not have to.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא; לְעוֹלָם כָּרָאוּי לִגְמַלִּים וּכְרָאוּי לִשְׁווֹרִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof of step 10 by reviving the case dismissed in step 9.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole proof from the 'covered properly … פטור' clause.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: It assumed a cover fit for camels gives an obvious ruling. In fact the ruling teaches something new: he did not need to knock on the cover to check it.
steps.confusionAlert: This clause now proves nothing either way about מגו. It is simply about a fully proper cover. The question from step 7 is finally settled in step 18.

steps.title: A new proof from the liable clause: what case does it mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings the משנה's next clause, 'did not cover properly … חייב', and starts working out its case. A cover too weak even for oxen cannot be meant, because then his liability would be obvious.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come hear: if he did not cover it properly, and an ox or donkey fell in and died, he is liable. What is the case? If you say the cover was not fit for oxen and not fit for camels, does it need to be said that he is liable?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new attempt at proof from the liable clause of the משנה. It starts setting up the case by ruling out the simplest one; the conclusion comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A cover too weak even for oxen makes him plainly negligent toward the ox that fell in, so the משנה would not need to say it. Ruling this out pushes us toward a cover fit for oxen but not camels, which is where the מגו question comes in.

keyTerms.meaning: Does it need to be said? (it is obvious)

phrases.english: Come hear:
If he did not cover it properly,

phrases.aramaic: וְנָפַל לְתוֹכוֹ שׁוֹר אוֹ חֲמוֹר, וָמֵת – חַיָּיב.
phrases.english: and an ox or a donkey fell into it and died, he is liable.
What is the case?
If you say it was not fit for oxen
and not fit for camels,
does it need to be said that he is liable?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the proof from the exempt clause failed, the גמרא turns to the liable clause of the same משנה.
steps.raayaObject: Whether we say מגו (the answer comes in step 13).
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה's clause 'did not cover properly … חייב'.

steps.title: The liable case must be a cover too weak for camels that rotted, so we do say מגו
steps.stepSummary: The case must be a cover fit for oxen but not camels. If camels are rare he would be אנוס and exempt, so camels must be common. If camels had weakened the cover, his liability would be obvious, so the case must be that it rotted. The משנה says חייב, so we do say מגו.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it must be fit for oxen but not for camels. Now, if camels are common, he is negligent, and if camels are not common, he could not have prevented it. Rather, camels must be common and the cover rotted from inside, and the משנה says he is liable. So we see that we do say: since he is negligent about camels, he is negligent about rotting too.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the proof from the liable clause. It narrows the case down step by step and concludes that we DO say מגו.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If camels are common and they weakened the cover, his liability would be too obvious to teach. So the proof reads the case as the cover rotting, while he was still negligent about the common camels. The משנה makes him liable even for the rotting, which is exactly מגו. This is the opposite of what step 10 tried to prove.

keyTerms.meaning: Could not have prevented it, an accident

phrases.english: Rather, is it not a case where it was fit for oxen
but not fit for camels?
Now, if camels are common, he is negligent,

phrases.aramaic: וְאִי דְּלָא שְׁכִיחִי גְּמַלִּים – אָנוּס הוּא!
phrases.english: and if camels are not common, he could not have prevented it!
phrases.notes: In that case he would be exempt, but the משנה says liable, so this option is out.

phrases.english: Rather, is it not where camels are common,
and it rotted from inside,
and the משנה teaches that he is liable?
Apparently we do say
that since he is negligent regarding camels,
he is negligent regarding the rotting!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא לָאו כָּרָאוּי לִשְׁווֹרִים וְלֹא כָּרָאוּי לִגְמַלִּים? וְאִי דִּשְׁכִיחִי גְּמַלִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the proof begun in step 12 by ruling out the other cases.
steps.raayaObject: That we do say מגו: negligence about camels makes him liable even when the cover rotted.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה's clause 'did not cover properly … חייב'.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix this up with step 10. That step tried to prove we do NOT say מגו and was pushed off. This step uses the other clause to try to prove we DO say מגו.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up a direct question for the sugya: can the owner be held liable for the rotting just because he was careless about something else (the camels)?

steps.title: The 'did not cover' case means camels weakened the cover
steps.stepSummary: The proof for מגו is rejected. The case is a cover fit for oxen but not camels, in a place where camels are common. Camels walked on it and weakened it, and then oxen fell in.
steps.simpleTranslation: They answered: No. The case really is a cover strong enough for oxen but not for camels, and camels are common there. Camels came and weakened the cover, and then oxen came and fell in.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof from step 13. It gives a new picture of the case so that the owner's liability does not depend on מגו.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 13 we pictured an ox falling only because the cover rotted, which would be liability through מגו. Now the cover was weakened by camels, and the owner should have expected that because camels are common there. So his own carelessness directly caused the oxen to fall, and no מגו is needed.

phrases.english: They said: No;
actually, it was covered properly for oxen
but not properly for camels,
and camels are common there;
and camels came and weakened it,
and oxen came and fell into it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרִי: לָא; לְעוֹלָם כָּרָאוּי לִשְׁווֹרִים וְלֹא כָּרָאוּי לִגְמַלִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof in step 13 by giving the case a different setting.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof for מגו from the 'did not cover properly … חייב' clause.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: It assumed the camel-weakening case was too obvious to be taught, so the case had to be rotting. Really the case is that camels weakened the cover, which is direct negligence, and step 15 explains why the משנה states it anyway.

steps.title: Why the משנה teaches an obvious case
steps.stepSummary: The new reading makes the חייב case obvious, since he is clearly negligent. The גמרא explains that the משנה only taught 'did not cover' to match its first clause, 'covered properly'.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what bothered you, that it is obvious because he is negligent: since the משנה taught the first clause 'he covered it properly', it also taught the last clause 'he did not cover it'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא deals with a problem its own answer creates: if the owner was plainly negligent, why does the משנה need to tell us he is חייב?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier (step 13) the גמרא set aside the common-camels case because the משנה would not teach an obvious ruling. Here it answers that the last clause is not teaching anything new. It is only there to balance the first clause, which does teach something.

keyTerms.meaning: Since, because (it taught one thing, it taught the other too)
First clause / last clause of a משנה

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the 'did not cover' clause teaches a new law here. In this answer it is only a matching partner to the first clause.

phrases.english: And as for what was difficult for you:
It is obvious, he is negligent!
Since it taught the first clause, "he covered it properly,"
it also taught the last clause, "he did not cover it."

steps.triggerLanguage: וּדְקָא קַשְׁיָא לָךְ – פְּשִׁיטָא, פּוֹשֵׁעַ הוּא!
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defends the reading in step 14 against the 'it is obvious' argument.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Stylistic: the last clause is taught only because the first clause was taught.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A משנה clause would not state an obvious ruling.
steps.terutzMaskana: The 'did not cover' clause can be obvious. It is there to match the first clause.
steps.whatToRemember: The משנה about covering the pit does not prove anything either way about מגו.

steps.title: A ברייתא about weak oxen and sharp oxen
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא. If a deaf, foolish, young or blind ox, or one walking at night, falls into the pit, the owner is חייב. If a sharp ox walking by day falls in, he is פטור.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: if a deaf ox, a foolish one, a young one, a blind one, or one walking at night fell into it, he is liable. If a sharp ox walking by day fell in, he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new proof for the מגו question from a ברייתא. This step only lays out the source, and the argument comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא separates animals that could not notice the pit from a sharp ox that should have seen it in daylight. For weak animals the open pit counts as negligence. For a sharp ox, the ox itself should have avoided the pit.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
If a deaf ox fell into it,
or a foolish one, or a young one,
or a blind one, or one walking at night, he is liable.
If it was a sharp ox walking by day, he is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: נָפַל לְתוֹכוֹ שׁוֹר חֵרֵשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the proof from the משנה fell away, a new source is brought.
steps.raayaObject: Whether we say מגו (careless in one way, so liable in every way).
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא contrasting weak oxen with a sharp ox walking by day.

steps.title: Why doesn't his carelessness carry over to the sharp ox?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the owner is פטור for the sharp ox. Since he is careless toward a deaf ox, he should also count as careless toward a sharp one.
steps.simpleTranslation: But why? Let us say: since he is negligent toward a deaf ox, he is also negligent toward a sharp ox!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא presses on the ברייתא with a question that is really a set-up for a conclusion. If מגו were true, the sharp-ox ruling would make no sense.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Leaving a pit open is negligence toward weak animals. If we said מגו, that negligence would make him liable for every animal, including the sharp ox. The ברייתא still says פטור, which points to the next step's conclusion.

phrases.english: But why is he exempt?
Let us say: since he is negligent with regard to a deaf ox,
he is also negligent with regard to a sharp ox!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאַמַּאי? נֵימָא מִדְּהָוֵי פּוֹשֵׁעַ לְעִנְיַן חֵרֵשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws out the implication of the ברייתא from step 16.
steps.raayaObject: That we do not say מגו.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא's exemption for the sharp ox, even though the owner was careless toward weak oxen.

steps.title: Conclusion: we do not say מגו
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes from the ברייתא that we do not say מגו. The owner is liable only for damage his carelessness actually caused.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, can we not learn from it that we do not say מגו? Yes, learn from it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא states its conclusion and confirms it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Being careless toward one kind of animal does not make him liable for an animal his carelessness did not endanger. The sharp ox should have seen the pit, so the owner is פטור for it.

keyTerms.meaning: Learn from it, conclude from it
Since: careless in one way, so treated as careless in every way

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא about the deaf ox and the sharp ox proves that we do not say מגו. A pit owner pays only for damage his carelessness actually caused.
steps.whyThisMatters: This settles the question the sugya has been working on. Liability follows the specific carelessness, not a general label of being careless.

phrases.english: Rather, is it not that we learn from it:
we do not say "since"?
Yes, learn from it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא לָאו שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ – לָא אָמְרִינַן מִגּוֹ? שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the argument begun in step 17.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: We do not say מגו. Negligence toward one kind of animal does not create liability toward an animal it did not endanger.

steps.title: רב explains 'forward' and 'backward'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא turns to the next case in the משנה, an ox that fell forward or backward into a pit because of the digging noise. רב says 'forward' means literally forward and 'backward' means literally backward.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'If it fell forward,' etc. רב said: 'Forward' means literally forward, and 'backward' means literally backward.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new line in the משנה and brings רב's explanation of its words. This opens a new discussion that continues afterward.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה rules that if an ox fell forward because of the sound of digging the digger is חייב, and if it fell backward he is פטור. רב reads 'forward' and 'backward' simply, as the actual direction the ox fell.

keyTerms.meaning: Etc. (the rest of the quoted line)

phrases.english: "It fell forward," etc.
phrases.notes: This quotes the next line of our משנה, about an ox frightened by the noise of digging.

phrases.english: Rav said:
"Forward" means literally forward,
"backward" means literally backward.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new topic: the גמרא moves on to the next clause of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In the משנה, 'forward' and 'backward' mean the actual direction the ox fell.
